opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions, and I don't believe the answer is that domain experts become less relevant. If anything, their role shifts upward.

Think about what a materials scientist spends their time on today. A lot of it is trial and error: synthesizing a candidate, characterizing it, finding it doesn't work, adjusting, trying again. It's slow and expensive, and a huge fraction of human effort goes into searching a gigantic space more or less by intuition. That's exactly the part that's getting automated. Generative models can propose candidates, simulation and machine-learned force fields can screen them far faster than before, and self-driving labs can close the loop experimentally.

But someone still has to decide what problem is worth solving and what "good" means. If you want a material that captures carbon from air, you have to specify stability, cost, manufacturability, toxicity, how it behaves after a thousand cycles. Those constraints are full of tacit knowledge that isn't in any database. The expert becomes more like an architect of the search: posing the right question, defining the objective, and recognizing when the model is confidently wrong.

That last point matters a lot. These models extrapolate, and in materials you're almost always out of distribution, because you're looking for something that doesn't exist yet. A domain expert looks at a proposed structure and says, "that will never be synthesizable," or "that's a simulation artifact." That judgment is incredibly valuable, and ideally you feed it back into the system so the models get better.

So I see it as a partnership. The machine handles the brute-force exploration, and the human brings physical intuition, taste, and responsibility for the outcome. The people who will thrive are those who learn to speak both languages, who understand the chemistry deeply and also know enough about the models to know when to trust them. Training that hybrid generation is, I think, one of the big challenges for universities right now.

And there's a bigger picture. We have problems, like climate change, where we simply cannot afford the twenty-year timeline it traditionally takes to bring a new material to market. Automation doesn't replace the expert. It gives the expert a much bigger lever.

r001.rationale: The response says experts do not become less relevant; their role shifts upward toward setting problems, guiding searches, and judging model outputs. It does not characterize their role as retreating.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the role gets more important, not less, but it changes shape quite a bit.

The naive picture is that you build a big generative model for molecules or crystals, you wire it to a self-driving lab, and the chemists and materials scientists become spectators. I don't believe that for a second, and I say that as someone who has spent a lot of time building exactly those kinds of models, both in academia and at Microsoft Research and now at CuspAI. The models are good at proposing. They are not good at knowing which questions are worth asking, and they are often wrong in ways that are obvious to an expert and invisible to the model.

So the first shift is from "doing the experiment" to "designing the search." A domain expert today spends a lot of time on the loop itself: synthesize, characterize, adjust, repeat. As that loop gets automated, their leverage moves upstream. What is the objective, really? If you ask a model to find a sorbent with high CO2 uptake, it will happily give you something that is thermodynamically beautiful and completely unsynthesizable, or that degrades in the presence of water, or that requires a precursor that costs more than the carbon it would capture. Encoding those constraints, deciding which ones are hard and which are soft, deciding what a good tradeoff looks like, that is deeply domain knowledge, and it is also the thing that determines whether the whole pipeline produces anything useful.

The second shift is toward being the model's critic. Our simulators, DFT and the neural network surrogates we train on top of them, are approximations. They have systematic failure modes. An experienced computational chemist can look at an energy landscape and say "that's suspicious, the functional is known to misbehave here," and that intuition is extraordinarily valuable as a prior for where to spend expensive validation budget. I think of the expert almost as part of the active learning loop, the component that tells you where the uncertainty estimates themselves can't be trusted.

Third, and this is the one I find most interesting, is that automation lets experts work at a different level of abstraction. When you can run ten thousand candidates through a simulator overnight, the question changes from "will this material work" to "what is the structure of the space of materials that work." That is a scientific question, not an engineering one, and it is a question that expert humans are much better placed to ask than a model that has no concept of what would be interesting to learn.

Now, there is a real cultural challenge here. A lot of the value of a domain expert has historically been tacit knowledge, things you learn in the lab that never make it into a paper. The automated systems can't absorb that unless someone writes it down, or better, turns it into data or into a constraint in the model. So part of the new job is translation: taking what you know and making it legible to a machine learning system. Some people find that enormously liberating and some find it threatening, and I understand both reactions.

And I'd add one caution from the ML side. There is a temptation for people like me to think that if we just make the models bigger and the data richer, the domain knowledge becomes redundant. I have been consistently humbled by that. The physics we build into these models, symmetries, conservation laws, the structure of chemical bonding, that all came from domain experts over centuries, and the models that work best are the ones where we were disciplined enough to respect it. So I see the future as a genuine collaboration, where the expert sets direction, encodes constraints, catches the model when it is confidently wrong, and gets to spend much more of their time on the parts of science that actually require a scientist.

r001.rationale: The candidate says domain experts become “more important, not less” as automation shifts them toward designing the search, critiquing models, and setting scientific direction. It does not characterize their role as progressively retreating.

astra-6.text:
I think the role shifts rather than disappears. As you automate more of the routine work—proposing candidates, running simulations, carrying out measurements—the domain expert can focus more on asking the right questions. What property do we actually want to optimize? What constraints matter? And what would constitute a useful discovery?

That expertise is also crucial when interpreting results. An automated system may find something that scores very well according to its objective, but an expert might recognize that it’s unstable, difficult to manufacture, or that the measurement is misleading. Equally, an unexpected result might be a clue to new physics rather than an error.

So I see it as a collaboration. The machines expand the space we can explore, and the experts help decide where to look and what the results mean. Ideally, that gives scientists more time to develop understanding, rather than simply producing more data.

r001.rationale: The response says that as more routine work is automated, experts shift away from doing it and focus more on framing questions and interpreting results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the role shifts from doing every step of an experiment to deciding which questions are worth asking. You can automate a lot of the loop—propose a material, simulate it, synthesize it, measure it—but you still need expertise to decide what you’re optimizing for and whether the measurements actually tell you what you think they do.

And when something unexpected happens, that’s often where the interesting science begins. Is it a problem with the experiment, a limitation of the model, or a new phenomenon? Domain experts are essential for making that distinction.

So I see this as a collaboration. Automation lets you explore more possibilities, and the expert helps turn that exploration into understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says experts shift away from doing every step as automation takes over much of the experimental loop, while focusing their effort on choosing questions and interpreting results.
